chunks: "I'd draw the MCU as a CPU in the middle connected through a bus matrix to everything else on the chip. The CPU core has registers, an ALU and a control unit, usually a pipeline.
On the bus it reaches on-chip flash, which holds the program, and SRAM for data and the stack.

Next to those are the infrastructure blocks: a clock subsystem with an internal oscillator, a crystal driver and a PLL with dividers feeding each peripheral; reset logic with power-on and brown-out detection; a voltage regulator for the core; and power modes.
The interrupt controller, like the NVIC on Cortex-M, delivers events to the CPU, and a DMA controller moves data between memory and peripherals without CPU work.
Then the peripherals: GPIO with pin multiplexing, timers and PWM, UART, SPI and I2C, ADC and DAC, comparators, a watchdog, an RTC, and a debug port such as SWD.
Everything is accessed through memory-mapped registers. A microprocessor has the CPU cores, which are fancier, with L1 and L2 caches and an MMU.
There's a memory controller to external DRAM, an interrupt controller, a bus fabric, boot ROM, and a set of high-speed and low-speed I/O blocks if it's an SoC.
But the working memory, boot storage and power-management chip are separate chips on the board.
A classic bare microprocessor, like an old 8086 or Z80, is just the CPU, with memory and I/O as external chips."
